A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendices E and G report original ViT and GPT-2 experiments on interpolation, expert matching, layer placement, and FFN reinitialization.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, with additional results for simultaneous all-layer MoE replacement and an expert-order matching ablation.

M1.justification: The two-stage algorithm remains unchanged: match experts using centered gating parameters or Gram-matrix representations, then align their internal neurons. Algorithm 1 moves from Appendix D.3 to Section 5.3; this is relocation, not a new procedure.

E1.justification: The vision, language-modeling, transfer-learning, and Appendix E reinitialization datasets and tasks are retained. The added experiments use existing datasets; their differences concern model configurations and comparison controls.

E2.justification: V2 Table 10 adds Skipping-Expert-Order Matching as a comparator to Total Weight Matching on One Billion Word. The original naive-interpolation and expert-versus-gate matching comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Section 6.2 and new Appendix G.3 substantially extend evaluation from individual MoE layer replacements to simultaneous replacement of all Transformer FFNs across ViT and GPT-2 configurations. Table 10 adds a control omitting expert-order matching. Appendix F also changes the reported CIFAR-10 pretraining optimizer from SGD to Adam, without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 10 extends analysis of the expert-order stage to One Billion Word, comparing full matching against skipping that stage across three MoE variants with four or eight experts. This supplements the earlier CIFAR permutation-ranking analysis. Existing FFN-reinitialization and depth-placement analyses remain.

E5.justification: The new all-layer experiment specifies six checkpoint pairs from four checkpoints, with endpoint metrics averaged over those four checkpoints. Table 10 specifies three independent checkpoint pairs. Existing repeated-run counts and uncertainty reporting remain unchanged; these additions do not establish increased repetition of earlier experiments.

E6.justification: New Table 7 adds all-layer loss and accuracy barriers and endpoint results across three MoE variants on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, and One Billion Word. Table 10 adds matching-ablation results, including loss barriers of 0.0053 versus 0.1384 for four-expert dense MoE. These are new comparisons, not cross-version performance gains. Table 4 also changes the Penn Treebank naive loss barrier from -0.0454 to 0.0454.

T1.justification: The group actions, functional-equivalence theorems, assumptions, counterexamples, and proofs in Sections 3–5 and Appendices A–D are retained. The metric formula added to Table 2's caption already appeared in Section 6.3.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about MoE symmetries, permutation alignment, and empirical LMC. The added experiments support the existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: Section 6.3 adds the interpretation that even minor expert-order mismatches can disrupt the shared representation space and interpolation smoothness. Existing explanations involving layer sensitivity and skip connections, and limitations concerning Top-1 routing and absent loss-barrier guarantees, remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds a public-code URL and newly documents ImageNet pretraining/fine-tuning epochs, warm-up and scheduling, One Billion Word training-step budgets and warm-up, and CIFAR-100's pretraining optimizer. These are additional disclosures, not evidence of changed budgets. Hardware and runtime information are retained; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Six references are added, principally an optimal-transport textbook and tree-sliced Wasserstein works, plus an equivariant graph-network paper cited in Appendix A. The paper's positioning relative to previous LMC and permutation-alignment research remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized experimental and implementation-description edits, moves Algorithm 1 into the main text, adds the all-layer subsection and NeurIPS checklist, updates author information, and replaces template acknowledgments with actual funding disclosures. Most scientific prose and the section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 introduces Tables 7 and 10, relocates Algorithm 1 and several existing displays, expands Table 2's caption, and reformats the title and author block. Existing figures and their plotted results are retained; much of the remaining visual difference is repagination.

improvement.justification: The all-layer evaluations reduce reliance on isolated-layer experiments, while Table 10 more directly tests the expert-order stage on language modeling. Added training schedules, code-access information, and the Table 4 sign correction improve reproducibility and accuracy. These are useful incremental gains, although appreciable residual barriers in the new all-layer language-model results still limit an unqualified interpretation of LMC.
